title: Leverage: how founders win at fundraising, sales, hiring and PR
summary: Dalton and Michael frame every startup negotiation around leverage: do you bring more value than you ask for, and could you walk away? Growth and a deep pipeline beat pitch decks, negotiation tricks and press. The pre-work is where the win happens.

principles.text: Leverage means bringing more value than you ask for; investors, customers and hires are not there to support you like teachers.
principles.quote: Do you bring something of value? Are you asking for more value than you can offer or are you delivering more value than you're asking for?

principles.text: Fundraising is won by growth and proof points, not deck polish; a bad fundraiser with traction beats a great one without.
principles.quote: the way to be very effective at fundraising is to be growing so quickly and have so many proof points that your startup is working

principles.text: Some investors string founders along for months as a free option, draining the time you need to build the inflection point.
principles.quote: The dark game theory is that the reason a lot of founders will get strung along for months is the investor is trying to see if they do start growing

principles.text: In sales, high leverage is heavy inbound so you can be picky; never depend on one deal, and keep doing outreach during a hot deal.
principles.quote: high leverage is that you have so much customer inbound that you can be picky and choosy.

principles.text: Hiring leverage comes from a deep pipeline; most founders have too few candidates at every stage.
principles.quote: I think when I'm debugging um founders hiring pipeline, the biggest issue is they don't have a pipeline.

principles.text: Treat hiring like sales: put in comparable effort, and move fast on good candidates, even handing a signed offer letter at the end of the last interview.
principles.quote: the amount of like emotional energy you have to put into hiring is on the level as getting customers because you're basically selling a job at your company.
